title: Gateless Barrier, Case 25: Yang-shan's Sermon from the Third Seat
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Gateless Barrier case 25, in which Yangshan dreams of Maitreya's palace, is seated in the third seat, and is called on to speak. Nomon asks how different dreaming is from waking, then tells a vivid dream of switching off a Dzogchen Ponlop Rinpoche recording, meeting Robert Thurman's smiling gaze, and leading metta phrases that kept coming out loud after waking. Nomon explains the weight of the third seat through the Shuso and monastic seniority, reads Zhuangzi on dreams, and tells how Wangyal Rinpoche met his teacher in a dream. Yangshan's sermon, that the truth of Mahayana is beyond proposition and denial, leads to holding views with an open hand and to the closing instruction to listen carefully.
topics: Zen koan about Master Yangshan's visit to Maitreya's palace

sentences.text: Nomon Kan, case 25, the 25th story in this collection of Zen stories.
*In a dream, Master Yangshan went to Maitreya's place and was led to sit in the third seat.
A senior monk struck the gavel and said, "Today the one in the third seat will speak."
Yangshan rose and, striking with the gavel, said, "The truth of Mahayana is beyond all propositions and denials.
Listen carefully, listen carefully."*
*In a dream, Master Yangshan went to Maitreya's place,* like a palace or a monastery, *and was led to sit in the third seat.
A senior monk struck the gavel and said, "Today the one in the third seat will speak."
Yangshan rose and, striking the gavel, said, "The truth of Mahayana is beyond all propositions and denials.
Listen carefully, listen carefully."*
This is a koan, and it takes place in a dream.
Have you had any dreams lately?
I always say "had dreams," as if they were something you could possess.
Have you experienced any dreams?
Have you been in a dream?
Dreams are fascinating, and maybe we do dreams a disservice, the way we dismiss them as just fantasies or weird stuff that the mind cooks up when we're sleeping, or we call them processing.
As I contemplated this story, I was wondering: are dreams really as different from waking as we think they are?
When we're awake, we take in sights and sounds and smells and touches and tastes, and we put all these sensory impressions together in our mind, along with a lot of other stuff, right?
With our history, our interpretations, our assumptions, our patterns.
And then in a flash we say, "Oh, this is reality."
I think we tend to think that, in the proportions of this process, almost all of it is sensory information from the real world that's out there.
Maybe I have to admit I put a little bit of a spin on it, because we're all a little biased.
There's always a little perception going on, but basically we're all perceiving the same waking reality.
That's what we assume.
But what if a lot more of that process is the mind than we think?

What if what we take for reality is actually mostly the assembly in the mind, mostly this rich combination of the past and random thoughts and images and memories and cultural myths and the things that are floating around in our subconscious and collective subconscious?
Buddhist psychology has a role to play for the collective subconscious.
I don't know if Jung knew about that or not.
But what if what we put together that we take for reality is not mostly the senses, not mostly an external reality, but actually mostly the mind itself?
And then in dreams we don't have as many outside inputs.
Our eyes are probably closed, but our ears are open, and we're feeling and we're in a body.
So maybe in a dream our mind does have a bigger role to play in the construction of reality that we're experiencing.
I wonder if it's as different as we think.
I had a vivid dream a few days ago which had a Buddhist theme, and here we are on a dream koan, so I thought I'd mention my dream.
I was inside a building, and behind and all around me it was dark, but in front of me there were a few steps up into a meditation hall, a small meditation hall.
So I stepped up into it, and I could see where I was.
There were no cushions, so I folded up my coat to sit on and sat down.
I sat down facing in, and to my right was a stereo, like an old receiver-type stereo on a little bureau or something.
The stereo was playing a talk by Dzogchen Ponlop Rinpoche, who is the teacher of Nalanda Bodhi in Seattle and many other places, a Tibetan teacher.
I met him once or twice.
And there's a woman sitting on my left, and I asked her if I could turn off the stereo so we could practice now, and she said okay, so I did.
I turned off Ponlop Rinpoche.
I wonder what that means.
And then I looked across this small hall, and right across from me, looking at me with a smile, was Robert Thurman.
You know Robert Thurman, an important American scholar of Tibetan Buddhism, and a practitioner too.
He was the first American ever ordained in a Tibetan order, ordained by His Holiness the Dalai Lama, who was an old friend of Bob Thurman's, someone I've also met once or twice.
I doubt he remembers me.
Bob Thurman is just an enthusiastic, positive guy, important in the Buddhist scene, and he's looking at me, and we have some kind of exchange.
I don't think he said anything, but somehow I knew that Bob approved of me, and was happy that I was there.
And then I started leading a metta meditation, a loving-kindness meditation.

I don't know if I was leading it out loud for this small group in the meditation hall or to myself, but the phrases I said to myself over and over on the breath were, "May I be happy, may I be peaceful, may I be happy, may I be peaceful."
That's a good phrase, huh?
May I be happy, may I be peaceful.
One interesting thing about the dream is that it happened after my alarm had gone off in the morning, and I think I woke up, and I think I was then dreaming.
I assume that I must have fallen back asleep, but that's an assumption.
I don't have any memory of falling back asleep.
I remember that the alarm went off, I was in bed, and then I was in this building.
Is it so simple as waking and sleeping?

And the other thing that's interesting is, once I did wake up in the usual way of waking up later, as I woke up, I was saying these phrases out loud: "May I be happy, may I be peaceful, may I be happy."
I couldn't stop saying them for quite a while, actually.
May I be happy, may I be peaceful.
It's like someone else was operating the body, operating the mouth.
So I had a dream like Master Yangshan, in which I got to practice.
Was I awake?
Was I asleep?
Does that place exist?
Does Maitreya Buddha's palace in the Tushita heaven, where this takes place, exist?
Is it all a fantasy?
I have some big decisions coming up in my life, and maybe you do too, and [unclear: "I'll do"].
I noticed I was trying to visualize what might happen if different choices were made.
Those are visions.
Those are dreams.
And we say they're not real.
But it's some way of the mind trying to understand reality, isn't it?
And then there are the people who have died, who it's not like they're gone.
They're right here.
We can perceive them, not with our usual way of perceiving, like we were awake.
We know they're here.
So in my dream I kind of knew I was dreaming, and that I was inside a dream.
I wasn't floating above it watching a movie.
Maybe I knew where I was sitting, and I could look around and do things.
I was worried when I turned off the stereo that it might fall over, and I might break it.
So who knows what's real in the end.
*In a dream Master Yangshan went to Maitreya's palace and was led to sit in the third seat.
A senior monk struck with the gavel and said, "Today the one in the third seat will speak."
Yangshan rose and, striking the gavel, said, "The truth of the Mahayana is beyond all proposition and denial.
Listen carefully.
Listen carefully."*
So we propose all kinds of realities, right?
And we deny all kinds of other realities.
Maitreya is the Buddha of the future, and he lives in this wonderful heaven.
It's the fourth of six heavens or something like that.
I'll get a little definition later.
It's where he practices and teaches and hangs out.
Beings in the Tushita heaven live a really long time.
And he's going to come to this world, but only after we've completely forgotten about Shakyamuni Buddha.
As long as we still remember Shakyamuni Buddha, Shakyamuni Buddha is still here.
And so there can only be one Buddha in any given world system in Buddhism.
This is like a far-out kind of talk.
The funny thing about it is that we know that Maitreya Buddha is there, but we won't be so surprised when he arrives, because he will only arrive once we've forgotten about Buddhas.
Once we've forgotten all about Buddhas, he'll know the world needs him or her now.
I don't know if Maitreya Buddha is gendered or not.
So even though we say Shakyamuni Buddha died, or Gautama Siddhartha or whatever his name was, even though we say he died 26 years ago, it seems he's not gone because we're here.
I've got a statue that references him behind my head.
So it seems Shakyamuni Buddha is still here.
So Maitreya Buddha has to stay in the Tushita heaven.

And when Master Yangshan, who is a Zen monk, a Chan monk, eighth century, we know his dates, he probably was a real person, when he arrived in Maitreya's monastery in the heavens, he was led to sit in the third seat.
That's a big deal.
Every year we have a powerful training opportunity called being the Shuso.
Somebody takes a special role during our winter eight-week practice period, a period of more intensive practice.
We have a Shuso.
And Shuso means first seat.
When I, as the teacher, get to welcome the new Shuso, in a very fun ceremony, which he or she tries to run away from, but they so far have not succeeded.
Anyway, after they get through the ceremony and they're being installed as Shuso, I say, "This student shares my seat and my responsibility.
Please help her lead us in the Dharma."
So the Shuso takes the first seat in the Zendo.
So in traditional Buddhism there's a lot of strictness about seniority.
Sometimes people think we're uptight, or sometimes I'm like, you have no idea.
This is mellow.
Everyone's always aware in a traditional Buddhist place what the order of seniority is.
You line up in order, you eat in order, and you sit in order.
Always in the same order, based on how long you've been practicing.
And the Zendo is not arranged exactly like this.
It's kind of a square that goes around a central figure, Manjushri, who would be in the middle.
And so there's a particular seat, right by where Ken is.
Ken is in the abbot seat, and Carrie is in the first seat.
And it goes around like that.
And then I'm afraid Wayne is the most junior monk.
Which, yeah.
It's a big deal, and so you can look around, and everyone's aware of this.
So the third seat is pretty high.
It's a big deal to enter a new monastery and be invited to sit in the third seat.
Maybe the person you bumped would be a little grouchy.
The abbot is sometimes out of order as they're appointed.
So Edie had to go rest, I assume.
I'm senior to Edie, but she's also senior to me.
She's been practicing far longer than I have.
So that's the significance of the third seat.
Presumably, to his surprise, after he sat down and the gavel was struck, there would be the tsuichin, like this post in the corner here, that we strike before important announcements.
So the yinno would have gotten up and struck the tsuichin, and then announced the talk.
Presumably Yangshan was surprised when the yinno said, "The third seat will speak tonight."
So, Spencer, you need to give the talk.
But you do not make excuses, right?
You do not demur.
You do not whisper that you haven't prepared anything and you're not ready and you're new here.
Really sorry.
I'm not worthy.
You wouldn't want to hear my talk anyway.
You get up and give the talk.
So Yangshan did.
He said, "The truth of Mahayana is beyond all propositions and denials.
Listen carefully.
Listen carefully."
Nobody said it had to be a long talk.
So, the truth of Mahayana.
Mahayana is the great way of Buddhism, or just the way, or just life, existence.
The truth of existence is beyond all propositions and denials.
Beyond anyone saying it's this, it's that, it's not this, it's not that.
And this so-called reality that we live in, we all know, is so fractured and messed up by propositions and denials, isn't it?
Did you watch any of the House's first public impeachment sessions, full of propositions and denials?
That's all it is, right?
Some of the denials are pretty funny, actually.
So basically that's what we do, full-time, 24-7, with ourselves and with each other.
We propose and deny.
Propose and deny.
What are we proposing?
What are we denying?
Reality.
Or realities.
I propose that I am me, and you are you.
You are not me, I am not you.
That is what I propose.
You want to deny it?
In half the time, or maybe all the time, it's denied.
And we are, all of us, so sure that our particular collection of propositions and denials is the right collection.
We're either super sure of that or we're super not sure of that, and either way it's a big problem for us to have these views that we hold.
A wonderful teaching from Zen is to let go of fixed views.
Don't hold fixed views.
Whenever consciousness is active, we're instantly generating views.
And there's nothing wrong with that.
It doesn't say, don't have views.
Do you notice that?
This little teaching, don't hold fixed views, is not the same as don't have views.
Views may come, views may go.
But don't lock them down.
Don't make them fixed.
Hold them with an open hand.
Don't be so sure.
Not knowing is most intimate, and so on and so forth.
Like the famous encounter, since we're in eighth-century China, we'll go back a few more centuries, the famous encounter with the Indian monk Bodhidharma, who shows up and is shown in to the emperor.
The emperor asks him all kinds of questions about Buddhism.
And the great visiting monk says, "I don't know."
That's the answer.
Don't know.
So that's not having a fixed view, or is it?
Is that a fixed view?
I don't know.
Or is it freedom from views?
We deny a lot too, right?
That's just fantasy, that's just a myth, that's just a story, that's just a lie.
Do we deny the reality of this place?
Do we deny the reality of the Tushita Heaven?
Do we deny the reality of my encounter with Bob Thurman?
I was talking to a friend of mine about that dream, and what I realized when I was talking to him is that Bob Thurman is an orthodox believer in the whole mythos of Tibetan Buddhism.
I mean, he's an educated American.
And he completely is certain and thinks that it's a mistake to dismiss rebirth and multiple levels of existence and multiple world systems.
That this is not just fantasy or myth, this is reality.
So I was thinking if I called him up and told him about this dream, he'd probably be really interested.
He'd probably talk to me a long time, some stranger.
But he would know I wasn't a stranger, right?
He would know that we had met.
And there's a whole branch, actually, of Tibetan Buddhism where you learn to be more awake, more lucid in your dreams.
Why?
So you don't lose all that practice time.
So you can practice throughout your sleeping time as well.
Isn't that wonderful?

He's got some great books about this, and I hope to get to practice with him one day.
Anyway, in one of his books he wrote that one time he was really perplexed about a problem, some choice he had to make.
And the only person who could help him was his teacher.
He knew that.
But his teacher was on a long retreat, and wasn't reachable by phone or Skype or anything like that.
So what Wangyal Rinpoche did was go to sleep with a strong intention to see his teacher.
And they did.
They met in the dream world and had a conversation.
And he got good support and advice from his teacher.
I haven't met Wangyal Rinpoche yet, but his books are very practical, very down-to-earth.
He mentions tie-ins to science and studies and stuff sometimes.
I think he's a very down-to-earth, smart, modern person who also is steeped in this reality, too.
So I have no reason to doubt him that he could travel in the dream world and visit his teacher.
I think that's probably true.
And our denial of that is mostly a lack of our imagination, probably.
So, dreams.
What's real?
What's the dream?
When we're awake, we think we know.
When we're dreaming, we're not so sure.
Chan Buddhism, and then later Zen, the Japanese name for the same thing, was influenced a fair bit, we think, by Taoism in China.
Everyone always says that.
I haven't really seen any scholarly evidence of that.
But everyone always says that, so it must be true.

Chu and you are both dreaming.
I say they're dreaming, but I'm dreaming too.

I don't know about that ending there.
The so-called kings, the so-called president, the so-called chairman select committee, the so-called Zen students, persist in their delusions.
Chu means like Jones, Smith or Jones.

The fool thinks he is dreaming.
Maybe one day we'll all wake up.

She said, this person said, the signs are there.
Next year we should wake up.
I'm all for it.
In some sutra I read about the Tushita Heaven.
There's a great long description.
I remember reading it was full of everything made out of jewels.
The trees made out of jewels, the mountains made out of jewels, the rivers made out of jewels.
Everything smells good.
You notice in all medieval mythology they often mention that it smells good.
It tells you what it usually smells like.
Here's an encyclopedia entry on the structure of the Tushita Heaven.
I thought you might be interested to learn a little bit about the Tushita Heaven, where Maitreya Buddha is waiting to help us out, and which Yangshan visited in a dream and got to give the talk.
*Tushita Heaven means Heaven of Satisfaction.
In ancient Indian and Buddhist cosmology there are desire heavens, non-desire heavens and space heavens.
The beings in this heaven are said to know satisfaction in the pursuit of pleasure, having transcended insatiable desire.*
The amazing thing about this world is that pleasurable things are actually satisfying.
*They have a life span of 4,000 years.
Each day of those 4,000 years is equal to 400 years in the human world.*
So it's 400 times 365 times 4,000 of our years.
There's a lot of math in this stuff too.
*It is said that Bodhisattvas are reborn in this heaven just before their rebirth in the world where they will attain Buddhahood.*
You're a really effective Bodhisattva.
You get one of these long pleasurable lives and then you're going to be a Buddha.
*Shakyamuni Buddha is said to have descended from this heaven and entered the womb of his mother, Maya.
The Tushita Heaven consists of an inner court and an outer court.
The inner court is the abode of Bodhisattva Maitreya, who is constantly preaching until his future rebirth in the human world as a Buddha.
Maitreya, along with the aspiration for rebirth in the Tushita Heaven, was popular in China in the 5th century, in Japan in the 7th century.*
They were like the Tushita Heaven cults.
Master Mumon has a lovely verse about this particular case.
He writes a verse about every one of them.
I don't share all of them.
The verse for this one is:
*Under the blue sky he preached a dream.
In a dream, absurd, how absurd, he deceived the entire assembly.
In broad daylight under the blue sky he preached a dream.
In a dream, how absurd, absurd, deceived the entire assembly.*

And your practice helps wake people up.
And Yangshan rose in Striking the Gavel said, *"The truth of Mahayana is beyond all propositions and denials.
Listen carefully, listen carefully."* Maybe this is the important part at the end.
Listen carefully.
Listen carefully.
Have care.
Really listen.
Whether you're in a dream or not, listen carefully.
